title: Your First Program
description: Every word in a Java program explained, line by line, so none of it is magic.

content.value: Here is a complete Java program. It prints one line. Every program you write starts from this shape.

parts.label: who can use it
parts.note: Anything is allowed to use this class.

parts.label: kind
parts.note: A **class** is a named container for code.

content.title: Line 1: the class
content.caption: The last `}` in the file closes this class.

parts.label: belongs to class
parts.note: The JVM can call it without building anything first.

parts.label: returns nothing
parts.note: It hands nothing back when it finishes.

parts.label: special name
parts.note: The JVM looks for `main` and starts here.

parts.label: inputs
parts.note: Room for words typed on the command line. You won't need it for a while, but `main` must have it.

content.value: Spell `main` wrong and the program still compiles, but it refuses to start. Nothing told the JVM where to begin.
content.title: The name matters

content.question: When your program starts, where does the JVM begin?
options: At the very first line of the file
content.explain: The JVM always looks for the method called `main` and starts running there.

parts.label: action
parts.note: Print this, then move to a new line.

content.value: Read `System.out.println` as a path, left to right: in the `System`, find its `out` (the screen), and tell it to `println`. Java is full of dotted paths like this.
content.title: Reading the dots

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: The quotes only mark where the text starts and ends. `println` prints what is inside them.

items: A file holding `public class Main` must be named `Main.java`, capitals included.
Every `{` needs a matching `}`. A one-line program still ends with two `}`.
Indent inner lines four spaces. Java doesn't require it, but it shows the nesting.
content.title: Rules to keep

steps.note: `{` opens the method `main`. The JVM starts running here.
This `}` closes the method. `main` is finished.
The last `}` closes the class. The program ends.

content.title: Braces in pairs
content.outro: The editor's file is already `Main.java`, so keep the class named `Main`. Try adding a third `println`: it prints exactly where you put it.

content.question: How many `}` does this one-line program end with?
content.explain: One closes the method and one closes the class.

practice.question: Print your own name on one line, then your favourite food on a second line. Two instructions inside `main`.
Print a three line message: Java is strict. / Braces come in pairs. / And I am fine with that. Each on its own line.

quiz.question: Where does the JVM start running your program?
options: At the first line of the file.
quiz.explain: The JVM looks for `main` by name and starts there. That is why the spelling of `main` matters so much.

quiz.question: Your class is `public class Player`. What must the file be called?
quiz.explain: The file name must match the public class exactly, capitals included. `Player` goes in `Player.java`.

quiz.question: What does `println` do that plain printing would not?
options: It moves to a new line after printing.
It prints in a larger size.
quiz.explain: The `ln` stands for line: it prints your text and then starts a new line, so the next output appears underneath.

quiz.question: How many closing braces does the smallest program need?
options: Two: one for the method and one for the class.
None, if the program is short enough.
quiz.explain: Each `{` needs its own `}`. The class opens one and the method opens another, so two must be closed.
